items.paragraph: A measurement can be precise without being accurate. If a scale consistently reads two kilograms too heavy, repeated weighings of the same object will agree closely with one another, and that agreement may inspire confidence, yet every reading is wrong by the same amount. Precision describes how tightly repeated results cluster; accuracy describes how close they lie to the true value. The distinction matters because the usual way of checking a result, repeating it, reveals only the first. A systematic error survives any number of repetitions untouched, and can be exposed only by comparing the instrument with an independent standard or a different method. Consistency is therefore reassuring about random noise but silent about bias.

items.paragraph: Procrastination is usually treated as a failure of time management, and the usual remedies follow from that diagnosis: calendars, lists, deadlines broken into smaller pieces. items.paragraph: Why do warnings that once alarmed people come to be ignored? The usual answer is that people grow careless, but the process is more reasonable than that. items.paragraph: Newspaper headlines have long had a grammar of their own: articles and linking verbs drop out, short words such as 'bid', 'probe' and 'row' replace longer ones, and the present tense is used for events that are already over. items.paragraph: The classic detective story asks the reader to accept an unusual bargain: every clue the detective uses must be shown on the page before the solution, so that a sufficiently attentive reader could, in principle, reach it first. A writer who must lay out every clue while still surprising the reader is tempted to reduce people to suspects and conversations to evidence, and many such books are remembered for their solutions rather than their characters. The finest examples avoid this by hiding clues inside character itself, so that understanding a person and solving the crime become the same act.

items.paragraph: Many people believe there is a moral difference between telling a lie and saying something true that is designed to mislead. items.paragraph: Two accounts of medieval craft guilds have long competed. On one, guilds were cartels: they restricted entry, fixed prices and kept outsiders from the trade, enriching masters at the expense of customers and would-be rivals. On the other, they were institutions of trust: in markets where buyers could not easily judge the quality of cloth or metalwork, a guild's standards and inspections gave its mark a meaning that no single workshop could establish alone. The two accounts are usually presented as rivals, but they describe mechanisms that can coexist in the same institution, and the more useful question is which one predominated under which conditions. Where quality was easy to observe, the trust function had little to add and restriction was likely to dominate; where quality stayed hidden until long after purchase, the same barriers to entry may have been the price of a reputation worth having.

items.paragraph: Counterfactual history, the study of what might have happened had some event gone differently, is often dismissed as a parlour game for historians with too much time. The dismissal overlooks that every causal claim in history is already a counterfactual. To say that a drought caused a rebellion is to say that without the drought the rebellion would not have occurred, or would have come later or smaller; a historian who refuses to think about alternatives cannot weigh causes at all. The real objection is to counterfactuals that stray far from the moment in question, imagining chains of consequences decades long, where every step multiplies uncertainty. Asking what was genuinely possible for the people involved, given what they knew and could do, is not fantasy but part of explaining why events took the course they did.

options.A: Traditional measures survived for so long because they were more logical than decimal units, being based on everyday tasks such as ploughing a field and carrying loads.
options.B: Decimal measurement was forced on unwilling populations by states and offered ordinary people no practical advantage at all over the local units that it replaced.
options.C: Decimal measures prevailed less through their logic than through state enforcement, as older units had real local uses, though the new system's convenience is not denied.

items.paragraph: Decimal systems of measurement are often presented as a triumph of reason over custom: once a simple, coherent set of units was available, the argument runs, the tangle of local measures was bound to give way. The history is less tidy. Traditional units were not merely clumsy; many were tied to things people actually did, a day's ploughing or a load a person could carry, and they let communities check trade by familiar standards. Where the new units spread, they often succeeded less through their logic than through the backing of states that needed uniform measures for taxation, armies and national markets, and they met long resistance where that backing was weak. None of this makes the decimal system less convenient; it suggests that its convenience was not, by itself, what made it prevail.

options.B: What a tip means depends on how staff are paid: where wages assume tips it is part of basic pay, but where full wages are paid it is a genuinely optional reward.
options.C: Customers should always tip generously wherever they travel, since a tip may form part of a worker's basic pay and withholding it can cause real harm to that worker.

items.paragraph: Tipping looks the same everywhere, a small sum left for good service, but it does quite different work in different places. Where wages for service staff are set on the assumption that tips will make up the difference, a tip is not a bonus at all; withholding it cuts the worker's basic pay, and the customer who tips carefully according to service is in effect setting a stranger's wage. Where staff are paid a full wage, the tip really is a discretionary reward, and leaving little or nothing is an ordinary judgement rather than a harm. Visitors who carry their home habits abroad therefore often get it wrong in both directions: they may seem mean in one country and needlessly lavish in another, since the same gesture carries a different meaning depending on how pay is organised.

options.B: Teaching a standard variety need not erase dialects, since people can use both; what endangers dialects is treating them as errors rather than as varieties.
options.C: Schools should stop teaching the standard form of the language, because doing so inevitably destroys the regional dialects that pupils bring with them from home.

items.paragraph: Schools that teach a standard form of a language are sometimes accused of destroying the regional dialects their pupils bring from home. The charge contains a truth: children who are told that their way of speaking is wrong often come to feel that it is, and may abandon it. But the fault lies in the telling, not in the teaching of the standard itself. Learning a second variety of one's language, useful in examinations, offices and correspondence with strangers, need not displace the first, any more than learning a second language erases one's mother tongue. Many speakers move between dialect and standard with ease, choosing according to company. What threatens a dialect is the attitude that treats it as a mistake, not the addition of another way of speaking.

options.B: A typist can record a lecture almost word for word, whereas a student writing by hand cannot keep up with the speaker and has to leave things out.
options.C: Students should always take lecture notes by hand, because typing on a laptop prevents them from learning anything from the lectures that they attend.
options.D: Handwritten notes aid memory because slowness forces students to select and rephrase, and typists who summarise rather than transcribe can gain much of the same benefit.

items.paragraph: It is often observed that students who take notes by hand remember a lecture better than classmates who typed nearly every word. The explanation is not that pens are magical but that they are slow. Unable to keep up with the speaker, the student writing by hand must decide what matters, compress it and put it in their own words, and this selecting and rephrasing is itself a form of learning. The fast typist can record the lecture almost verbatim without having to think about it at all. The advantage, then, belongs to the mental work rather than to the instrument, and a typist who deliberately summarises instead of transcribing can recover much of it.

options.A: Cursive should continue to be taught because forming letters by hand helps young children learn to recognise them, which is a benefit that typing on a keyboard cannot provide.
options.B: Schools should stop teaching handwriting altogether, because keyboards are what adults actually use and the supposed benefits of cursive are rarely supported by evidence.
options.C: The cursive debate merges two questions: the fairly strong case for teaching handwriting does not carry over to the joined style, whose particular benefits are less well supported.
options.D: The debate over cursive is at bottom a contest between tradition and efficiency, and efficiency should prevail because most adult writing is now done on keyboards.

items.paragraph: Debates over whether schools should still teach joined-up handwriting are usually framed as a contest between tradition and efficiency: cursive is a heritage skill, keyboards are what adults actually use. The framing obscures the fact that the two sides are often talking about different things. The case for teaching some handwriting is fairly strong, since forming letters by hand appears to help young children learn to recognise them, and much early schoolwork is still done with a pencil. But that case is about handwriting in general, not about the particular joined style, and an argument for one is easily mistaken for an argument for the other. The case for cursive specifically rests on weaker grounds: claims that it is faster, or that it builds discipline, are rarely as well supported as their advocates assume. A school could therefore drop cursive and keep handwriting without any inconsistency.
